newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military stays in Haiti pending U.N. decision.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military stays in Haiti pending U.N. decision.

text.p: The head of U.S. military forces in Latin America and the Caribbean said on Wednesday that the U.S. military support group in Haiti will continue to operate pending a U.N. decision on whether to extend its presence there beyond July 31.
"The U.N. has not made a decision yet on whether to extend past 31 July the U.N. presence," Gen. Wesley Clark told Reuters.

"It is my understanding that diplomatic discussions are, or shortly will be, under way to review these matters and in the meantime, U.S. military support is continuing to perform its function very well," he said.
Military personnel in Haiti had not been informed of any final decision on whether U.S. military personnel would stay, he added. The group's mission formally expired on June 1.

Military aides said that if the mandate of the U.S. troops was extended at least until the end of 1997, the group's strength would remain around recent levels of some 500 personnel. They declined comment on what would happen to the U.S. presence in Haiti if the United Nations leaves, saying the question was hypothetical.
Clark heads U.S. Southern Command, which is in charge of all U.S. military activities in Latin America except Mexico. Southern Command took over Caribbean responsibility on June 1.

Foreign troops have been patrolling Haiti since September 1994 when a force of 20,000 U.S. troops led an occupation that ended a military dictatorship and restored the Caribbean nation's elected government.

The support group includes airborne infantry soldiers from the U.S. Army's Fort Bragg, who carry out security functions, and medical and engineering units dedicated to humanitarian tasks such as road building and school renovations.
Diplomatic, military and police sources have said U.S. military personnel were also taking part in drug interdiction efforts in Haiti.

"What the Department of Defence does is provide information, training, planning, assistance and logistics support for U.S. law enforcement agencies and host nations who are engaged in the fight against narcotrafficking," Clark said.

Haiti's streets are being patrolled by 700 Canadian soldiers and 500 Pakistani troops funded by the United States. An estimated 300 U.S., French, Canadian and Algerian police officers are training the Haitian National Police.
Haitian organisations have demonstrated in recent months against the foreign military presence, which they view as an occupation of their country.
